label: Kimi K3.1 Pro
output:
### Four stars — a real improvement for our livestream, with some limitations

**Our rating: 4 out of 5 stars.**

I’m a Lutheran pastor, not an engineer, so this is a congregation’s review rather than a technical one. We bought the Lindqvist Optics PT-20 from Chancel AV in February 2026 for $2,140, plus another $95 for the wall mount. It replaced the webcam we had been using to livestream worship since 2020.

Our nave is 92 feet long, and the camera is mounted at the back on the balcony rail. That distance is where the PT-20 has earned its keep. The 20x optical zoom gives us a clear view of the chancel without making everything look like it was photographed from another county. The camera’s 1080p60 picture is a substantial improvement over our old webcam. Delores, an 82-year-old homebound member, called to tell us she could finally read the hymn numbers on the board. That phone call told us more about whether the purchase was worthwhile than any specification sheet could.

PoE allowed us to run one network cable up to the balcony for power and the camera connection. We use NDI HX to bring the picture into OBS on our old office PC, which streams to our YouTube channel. Most Sundays, we have between 30 and 60 viewers. The camera also has a regular HDMI output, although we have not needed it.

We have stored nine presets: altar, pulpit, lectern, font, choir loft, piano, a wide view, and two positions for the chancel steps. Erik, our 16-year-old acolyte, operates the camera through the free web app on a tablet. He learned it in one afternoon. I would not describe the whole system as effortless, but a volunteer should not be afraid of it.

It was not perfect out of the box. On our first Sunday, the presets drifted a few degrees by the time we reached the sermon. That was irritating, particularly since we had just spent a considerable amount of money for a small congregation. A firmware update to version 2.4 in March fixed the problem, and the presets have stayed where we put them since then.

Low-light performance is better than we had any right to expect from the old webcam, but it is not miraculous. At our Easter Vigil in April, during the first singing of “Christ the Lord Is Risen Today” with only candlelight, the picture became grainy. It remained usable, and we could still follow the service. The old webcam would have shown little more than dots.

The autofocus can hunt when someone walks between the camera and the pulpit. Our workaround is to lock the focus on the presets. That works for us, but it is something to understand before depending on the camera during a service. The manual is thin and badly translated. Fortunately, Chancel AV’s phone support was excellent. Marcy was patient, clear, and did not make me feel foolish for asking basic questions.

One other thing deserves emphasis: **this camera did nothing for our sound problem.** That is not its job. If people watching at home cannot hear the readings clearly or complain that the music sounds muffled, a better camera will not solve it. Sound needs its own attention and possibly its own budget.

Would I buy the PT-20 again? Yes, for our long nave and our particular needs. It has made worship more accessible to people who cannot be with us in person, and the improvements are visible to ordinary viewers. But I would not tell every congregation under 100 that it needs to spend this much. A church with a smaller room and simpler requirements may do perfectly well with something cheaper.

This has been a very good upgrade for us, provided you understand what it does—and what it does not do.
